morning_soundtrack.title: Victoryland – “The Ugliest Girl On The Beach”
morning_soundtrack.snippet: We here at Stereogum are big fans of Victoryland, the partnership of singer-songwriter Julian McCamman (ex- Blood ) and producer Dan Howard (also of the special new band Billboard Style). Also fans of Victoryland: Dead Oceans, one of the biggest and best labels in indie music, which has just added the band to their roster.
morning_soundtrack.vibe_check: Salt-stung and sun-bleached, like a lo-fi daydream drifting just past the shoreline.

morning_soundtrack.title: Michael Shannon & Jason Narducy Announce Tour Covering R.E.M.’s Document For Its 40th Anniversary
morning_soundtrack.snippet: At this point, it's an annual tradition: The acclaimed, intense, Oscar-nominated actor Michael Shannon heads out on tour with his indie rocker buddy Jason Narducy, and they pay tribute to a different classic IRS Records-era R.E.M. album. Actual members of R.E.M. sometimes join them. A couple of times, this has led to unofficial R.E.M. reunions .
morning_soundtrack.vibe_check: The warm, slightly surreal feeling of watching old friends argue passionately about a band you all loved before life got complicated.

morning_soundtrack.title: Future Sounds Of Jazz Vol. 16
morning_soundtrack.snippet: Future Sounds of Jazz Vol. 16 is both a forecast and a wormhole. Across two discs, Michael Reinboth and Michael Rütten move through jazz, dub, electronic music, improvisation, and psychedelia with the intuitive logic of a late-night DJ set. The result is a strange, elastic universe of DJ Oil, Bitchin Bajas, Booker Stardrum, Nico Zam, Ilhan Ersahin, and Momoko Gill—and a reminder that the future of jazz remains gloriously undefined.
morning_soundtrack.vibe_check: The feeling of a city blurring past a taxi window at 2am, every genre bleeding into the next like neon on wet pavement.

global_silver_linings.title: Good News in History September 30
global_silver_linings.snippet: 163 years ago, George Bizet’s famous opera Les Pêcheurs de Perles, The Pearl Fishermen, debuted at the Théâtre Lyrique in Paris. Set in ancient times on the Island of Sri Lanka, it tells the story of how two men’s vow of eternal friendship is threatened by their love for the same woman, whose own dilemma […]
global_silver_linings.reason: History is full of quiet turning points and forgotten kindnesses worth remembering — a daily reminder that progress has always been built by ordinary people doing extraordinary things. Looking back can be one of the best ways to find the courage to move forward.

global_silver_linings.title: Public speaking expert shows how the 3-part structure of Madonna’s VMA speech can be used by anyone
global_silver_linings.reason: The ability to speak clearly and connect with an audience is a skill anyone can learn, and breaking it down into a simple structure puts that power within everyone's reach. Confident communication opens doors that talent alone often cannot.

global_silver_linings.title: What We’re Reading: Rat Rangers to the Rescue
global_silver_linings.snippet: Welcome back to our weekly behind-the-scenes glimpse at what’s getting our team talking. Tell us what you’ve been reading at info@reasonstobecheerful.world and we just might feature it here. Rat tales With the rat population growing in Washington, D.C., a group of residents is working to educate their neighbors about ways...
global_silver_linings.reason: Rats are among the most misunderstood creatures on Earth, and stories of people working alongside them — whether in conservation or detection work — remind us that compassion and curiosity can reshape our relationship with even the most unlikely animals. It's a small but genuine sign that we're learning to see the world through a wider lens.

global_silver_linings.title: Why noise is an underestimated health hazard and what to do about it
global_silver_linings.snippet: BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM Most of the damage noise does to your body is preventable, and the tools you need are either free or already in your pocket. The missing piece, for most people, is understanding what counts as too much. Noise is an environmental health hazard that rarely gets treated as one.
global_silver_linings.reason: Recognising noise pollution as a serious health issue is the first step toward quieter, calmer communities — and the fact that solutions already exist is genuinely encouraging. Advocating for stillness is, in its own way, an act of care for everyone around us.

discovery_articles.title: 23rd Street Mural in Austin, Texas
discovery_articles.snippet: Painted in 1974 on the side of a building near the University of Texas campus, the 23rd Street Mural looks at first like a gloriously weird artifact from old Austin. Look closer and things get stranger. Its sprawling cast of characters, creatures and landmarks includes real people, legendary clubs, armadillos, political movements, underground comics, a health-care revolution, Willie Nelson, moon towers, peyote, and plenty of things that require some explaining.
discovery_articles.ferns_note: What looks like a tie-dyed fever dream on a Austin brick wall is actually a dense, hand-painted encyclopedia of counterculture — the kind of mural where armadillos share space with healthcare revolutionaries and you keep finding new faces the longer you stare. It's less a painting than a neighborhood's subconscious, frozen in 1974.

discovery_articles.title: MRI Scans Might Reveal Signs of Alzheimer's Disease Seven Years Before a Telltale Marker Appears in the Brain
discovery_articles.snippet: Not all researchers are convinced that the brain changes detected via MRI are robust enough to become a diagnostic tool. But the findings could help researchers better understand the mechanisms that drive the neurodegenerative disease
discovery_articles.ferns_note: The quietly staggering implication here: Alzheimer's may be rewriting the brain's architecture nearly a decade before the disease announces itself through its usual calling cards. If the findings hold, the window for intervention could shift dramatically — and so could everything we think we know about when this disease actually begins.

discovery_articles.title: In One of Rome’s Most Famed and Neglected Villas, Centuries-Old Risqué Frescoes, Painted Over by Nuns, Have Reappeared
discovery_articles.snippet: Nearly a year into a $40 million restoration of the Villa Silvestri Rivaldi, conservators are rediscovering and reviving 16th-century art
discovery_articles.ferns_note: Somewhere between the 16th century and a convent's sense of propriety, a coat of whitewash buried frescoes that were apparently too risqué for holy women to live alongside — and now, after centuries of patient concealment, the paintings are simply reappearing. There's something delicious about the nuns losing this particular argument to time.

discovery_articles.title: Japan's Smallest and Least-Populated Major Island Is a World of Pilgrimages, Delicious Food and Plenty of Forest Bathing
discovery_articles.snippet: Each year, more than 100,000 people hike at least part of a 750-mile route on Shikoku that connects 88 Buddhist temples and other sacred sites
discovery_articles.ferns_note: Shikoku's 750-mile pilgrimage circuit is one of the world's great walks, yet it remains gloriously under-romanticized in the Western imagination — 88 temples, deep forest, and a tradition of *ohenro* walkers who are still offered food and shelter by strangers as a matter of spiritual custom. It's a reminder that some of the oldest forms of hospitality are also the most quietly radical.

discovery_articles.title: In 1884, Gale-Force Winds Ran a Ship Aground Near Cape Cod. Now, the Nor’easter Lashing the East Coast May Have Uncovered Part of It
discovery_articles.snippet: The wreckage could belong to the “Warren Sawyer,” a three-masted cargo schooner that foundered more than 140 years ago
discovery_articles.ferns_note: A nor'easter just did what 140 years of tides couldn't quite finish — strip away enough sand to reveal the bones of a three-masted schooner that went down in an 1884 gale and has been slowly surfacing ever since. The sea, it turns out, is an unreliable keeper of secrets.

featured_read.title: You Should’ve Said Something
featured_read.snippet: "I had to do everything the jurors did—sit in every court session, examine each piece of evidence, look out from the jury box every day at a man accused of murder—but I wouldn’t participate in the deliberation unless two jurors dropped out."
featured_read.blurb: What does it mean to witness a murder trial in full — every grim detail, every human face — and yet be denied the final act of judgment? This essay sits with the strange, suspended guilt of the alternate juror.

reading_room.title: The Real Technofascists of Silicon Valley: Why Big Tech Oligarchs Hate Democracy
reading_room.snippet: When I first started seeing coverage of what seemed like a deranged plan from the Trump administration to take over Greenland, I felt like I was losing my mind. Not because I didn’t understand the plot, but because none of
reading_room.blurb: The ambitions of Silicon Valley's most powerful men have outgrown mere disruption — this piece traces the ideological thread connecting tech oligarchy to a genuine contempt for democratic self-governance, and asks why we're so slow to name it.

reading_room.title: Noema’s AI Reading List
reading_room.blurb: A reading list is only as good as its curation — but with no snippet to go on, this one stays behind the curtain for now.

reading_room.title: Why Did Wallace Shawn Liken Israelis to Nazis?
reading_room.snippet: The people casually accusing Israel of genocide
reading_room.blurb: Wallace Shawn's provocation opens onto a harder question: what do we owe the precision of language when the stakes are this high, and who gets to decide when a comparison crosses from critique into cruelty?

reading_room.title: The Mysteries of Human Personality
reading_room.snippet: Robert Kolker’s latest book, The Vanishing Family , tracks the effects of inherited dementia and the many transformations that follow.
reading_room.blurb: Robert Kolker follows a family undone by inherited dementia, asking what remains of a person — and of the people who love them — when memory and personality quietly dissolve.

reading_room.title: So You Think You Could Be An Electrician?
reading_room.snippet: Funny how the people telling kids to get jobs in the trades tend to be white-collar.
reading_room.blurb: The advice to "learn a trade" comes cheap from those who never will — this essay digs into what the skilled-trades pipeline actually looks like from the inside, and who bears the real cost of our romantic notions about it.

garden_note.note: There's a particular quality to the light at this turning of the year in Zürich — slanted and golden even by mid-morning, catching the first blush of colour in the maples along the Limmat. Step out after 06:53 and you'll find the garden draped in that quiet, dew-heavy stillness that only early autumn delivers.
in_season: Dahlias: still flowering gloriously — cut stems for a last vase before the first frost threatens
Quince: harvest time is here, the heavy yellow fruits ready to pull from the branch
Kale and leeks: thriving in the cooler air, sweeter now after the first chilly nights
Clearing spent summer beds and working in compost before the ground hardens
garden_note.sky_tonight: The waning gibbous moon rises well after midnight — look for Saturn in the south-eastern sky during the early evening hours, still shining steadily in Aquarius.
garden_note.sun_times: First light creeps in at 06:53 this morning, and the sun sets at 19:09 — savour those last warm hours in the garden.
